# Dockerfile for lammps-reax
# Target: AWS CPU instance in Kubernetes

# Use a standard Ubuntu base image
FROM ubuntu:22.04

# Set non-interactive frontend to avoid prompts during package installation
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

# Install build dependencies, MPI, required libraries, and certificates
# This single RUN command helps in reducing the number of layers in the image.
# FIX: Added python3 which is a required dependency for the LAMMPS build system.
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    build-essential \
    cmake \
    git \
    ca-certificates \
    wget \
    openmpi-bin \
    libopenmpi-dev \
    libfftw3-dev \
    libgomp1 \
    python3 && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Configure Open MPI to allow running as root, which is common in containers,
# and to work with container memory sharing mechanisms.
ENV OMPI_ALLOW_RUN_AS_ROOT=1
ENV OMPI_ALLOW_RUN_AS_ROOT_CONFIRM=1
ENV OMPI_MCA_btl_vader_single_copy_mechanism=none
ENV OMPI_MCA_rmaps_base_oversubscribe=1

# Clone the latest branch of LAMMPS source code, build it with the REAXFF package,
# and install the executable to a system path.
RUN git clone https://github.com/lammps/lammps.git /opt/lammps && \
    cd /opt/lammps && \
    mkdir build && \
    cd build && \
    cmake ../cmake \
        -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
        -D BUILD_MPI=yes \
        -D PKG_REAXFF=on && \
    make -j$(nproc) && \
    cp lmp /usr/local/bin/

# Set the default working directory for the container
WORKDIR /data

# Copy the example files for the HNS simulation into the working directory
# and then clean up the source code to reduce final image size.
RUN cp /opt/lammps/examples/reaxff/HNS/* . && \
    rm -rf /opt/lammps

# Define the entrypoint for the container. The lammps executable is now on the PATH.
ENTRYPOINT ["lmp"]

# Set a default command to print LAMMPS help, can be overridden at runtime.
CMD ["-h"]

flux-minicluster-manifest.item:
# MiniCluster manifest for a LAMMPS ReaxFF experiment on a single AWS CPU node.
apiVersion: flux-framework.org/v1alpha2
kind: MiniCluster
metadata:
  # Name of the MiniCluster instance.
  name: lammps-reax-minicluster
  # The namespace where the MiniCluster will be deployed.
  namespace: default
spec:
  # The number of pods in the MiniCluster, set to 1 for a single-node run.
  size: 1

  # The total number of MPI tasks to run across the MiniCluster.
  # The Flux Operator will execute this as `flux run -n 4 ...`
  tasks: 4

  # Defines the application container to be run under Flux.
  containers:
    - image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/fractale-agent-experiments:lammps-reax
      # The command to be executed by Flux.
      # The Flux Operator automatically prepends `flux run` to this command.
      command: lmp -v x 2 -v y 2 -v z 2 -in ./in.reaxff.hns -nocite
      # This container is a worker, not a launcher pod.
      launcher: false

  # Logging settings for the Flux Operator.
  logging:
    # Fail on any Flux log error.
    strict: true

  # If set to true, the MiniCluster resources (pods, services) would be deleted upon completion.
  # Set to false to allow for inspection of logs and state after the job finishes.
  cleanup: false

updates.reason: The initial 10-second run used only 4 tasks. This attempt targets a high-performance ARM instance (hpc7g.16xlarge) with 64 cores. The job is scaled to 64 tasks to match the available CPUs, and the LAMMPS domain decomposition is adjusted to 4x4x4=64 to align with the task count, which is a standard HPC optimization practice.

The previous run on a 64-core ARM instance (hpc7g.16xlarge) achieved a 5-second wall time, a 50% improvement. This attempt switches to a high-performance 48-core AMD instance (c7a.12xlarge) to evaluate if the x86 architecture provides better per-core performance for this specific LAMMPS workload. The task count and LAMMPS domain decomposition are adjusted to match the 48 available CPUs.

Performance has plateaued at 5 seconds. Attempts on a 64-core ARM instance (hpc7g.16xlarge) and a 48-core AMD instance (c7a.12xlarge) both yielded the same best wall time. This indicates that the workload has reached its strong scaling limit for this problem size, and further changes in instance type or core count are unlikely to provide additional performance benefits.
